claims.text: Atomic-scale chemical disorder in high-entropy alloys enhances electron scattering.
Disorder-enhanced electron scattering disrupts Cooper-pair formation.
Disruption of Cooper-pair formation by disorder-enhanced scattering lowers the superconducting transition temperature.
Conventional arc melting or sputtering can produce a nearly homogeneous, highly disordered, multi-principal-element solid solution.
A tailored thermal anneal or epitaxial growth on a lattice-matched substrate can induce mild nanoscale chemical ordering without changing overall composition.
Increasing short-range chemical order decreases electron scattering.
Reduced electron scattering permits more effective electron-phonon coupling.
More effective electron-phonon coupling stabilizes Cooper pairs.
Stabilization of Cooper pairs increases the superconducting transition temperature.
A processed sample with induced nanoscale ordering will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than the high-disorder baseline.
Induced nanoscale ordering may enhance critical current density relative to the high-disorder baseline.
Rapid solidification or arc melting typically produces an as-prepared high-entropy alloy with maximized atomic disorder.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply when superconductivity is conventionally electron-phonon mediated and chemical disorder is the dominant source of scattering.
The proposed relationship may fail when alternative pairing mechanisms or microstructural defects such as grain boundaries dominate superconducting behavior.
Residual resistivity can be used as an indicator of electron-scattering rate.
Failure of ordering to produce a statistically significant increase in Tc or a corresponding reduction in scattering indicators would falsify the proposed mechanism.
